abstract: ATG8 proteins are key regulators of autophagosome biogenesis and maturation. Despite extensive research on human ATG8 family members, the functional differences between individual proteins remain poorly understood. Among them, LC3C is one of the least characterized members. However, its involvement in a growing number of cellular processes has attracted increasing interest in understanding its specific functions. Here, we investigated the functional specialization of LC3C using HeLa ATG8 Hexa-knockout cells individually reconstituted with GFP-LC3C or GFP-LC3B. This experimental system allowed us to examine the specific properties of each protein independently of other ATG8 family members. Under starvation conditions, LC3C formed more numerous and larger autophagic vesicles than LC3B, while both proteins sustained autophagic flux. Furthermore, proteinase K protection assays confirmed that both proteins could promote autophagosome closure. The two proteins also differed in their ability to promote the autophagic degradation of specific cargo receptors, with LC3B being more efficient in p62 degradation and LC3C in NDP52 degradation. Confocal microscopy revealed that LC3B and LC3C predominantly localized to distinct autophagic vesicles, suggesting their association with different autophagosome subpopulations. Finally, analysis of chimeras generated by exchanging regions between LC3B and LC3C revealed that the N-terminal region of LC3C determines autophagic vesicle size, whereas its ubiquitin-like core influences intracellular localization. Together, these results suggest that LC3C contributes to determining specific autophagosome properties, such as their size and intracellular localization, expanding our understanding of how individual ATG8 proteins regulate the autophagic process.
